content.prompt: Part 1 — Ausable and Max
content.answer: The story is set in a small, unimpressive hotel room in Paris. Ausable, a fat and sloppy secret agent, is talking to Fowler, a young and romantic writer who had hoped for some adventure with a real spy. Fowler is disappointed: Ausable seems nothing like a glamorous secret agent — he is fat, speaks with an accent, lives in a cramped sixth-floor room and is concerned only about the dinner he has ordered. Suddenly, a man with a gun, Max, appears at the door. He tells Ausable he has come to get a report that is supposed to be in Ausable's room, and to deal with the agent.

content.prompt: Part 2 — The quick thinking
content.answer: Ausable is taken by surprise but recovers quickly. He pretends to be angry that the report has not yet been delivered, and he calmly tells Max that the report will be brought to his room in a few minutes. Then he mentions, almost casually, that his room has a balcony — and that the balcony extends along the side of the building to the window of the next room. He adds that nobody has ever dared to use it, because it is dangerous: rooms on this floor are hard to enter that way. Max believes him and grows nervous.

content.prompt: Part 3 — The fall
content.answer: Ausable, still calm, invents a noise outside — a knocking at the door — and declares that it must be the police, who have come to arrest Max. Terrified, Max decides to escape through the window onto the balcony. He climbs out, but as he goes, there is a cry and a thud below. When Ausable opens the door, there is no one there — it was a waiter arriving. Ausable then reveals to Fowler the trick: this room has no balcony. Max, in his fear, stepped out of the window and fell to his death.

content.prompt: Part 4 — The secret of the agent
content.answer: Ausable explains to the amazed Fowler that the report he mentioned does not exist — it was pure invention, used to keep Max calm. His real "secret", he says, is that he is a man who is "too fat" and cannot act quickly, so he must use his mind: thinking fast is his weapon. Fowler, who had been disappointed by Ausable's ordinary appearance, now sees the true skill of the agent: not glamour or action, but quick, cool thinking under pressure. The story ends with Fowler's respect and the waiter announcing dinner.

content.prompt: Presence of mind and quick thinking
content.answer: The central theme is the power of presence of mind. Ausable wins not with weapons or strength but with rapid, cool-headed invention — a fictional balcony, a fictional report, a fictional knock. In dangerous moments, the story suggests, the mind is the greatest weapon; calm intelligence beats brute force.

content.prompt: Appearances can be deceptive
content.answer: The theme of deceptive appearances runs through the story. Ausable looks like a comically unfit, forgetful clerk — nothing like a glamorous spy — yet he outwits the armed intruder with ease. Fowler learns that heroism is not a matter of looks or gadgets but of intelligence and courage. The story warns against judging people by appearances.

content.prompt: Ausable
content.answer: Ausable is a secret agent who defies every stereotype: he is fat, sloppy and lives in a cramped, unimpressive room in Paris. He speaks with an accent, orders dinner with relish and seems more like a middle-aged clerk than a spy. But his genius is his mind. Surprised by an armed intruder, he thinks faster than Max can act, inventing a balcony, a nonexistent report and a knock at the door to trap his enemy. His own "secret", he says, is that being too fat to act quickly, he learned to think fast instead. He is witty, cool and brilliantly resourceful — proof that the quietest man can be the deadliest.

content.prompt: Max
content.answer: Max is the enemy agent with a gun and a mission: to take the report that he believes is in Ausable's room. He is confident and menacing at first, dismissing Ausable as a fool, but he is also gullible and nervous. Ausable's calm story about the dangerous balcony unsettles him, and the imaginary knock at the door panics him completely. In his fear, he climbs out of a window that leads to a six-storey fall — his own greed and credulity destroy him. Max represents the enemy who relies on force and is defeated by intelligence.

content.prompt: Fowler
content.answer: Fowler is a young writer who has come to meet a real secret agent, dreaming of glamour and adventure. He is bitterly disappointed when Ausable turns out to be fat, ordinary and obsessed with dinner. Through his eyes, the reader sees Ausable's unimpressive exterior — and, at the climax, his extraordinary mind. By the end, Fowler has learned the lesson of the story: true adventure lies not in appearance but in quick thinking. He is the reader's stand-in, moving from scepticism to admiration.

content.prompt: Stay calm in a crisis
content.answer: The story teaches the value of keeping one's head in a crisis. When Max appears with a gun, Ausable does not panic or fight — he thinks, and his calm invention of a balcony, a report and a knock saves his life. The lesson is that panic destroys judgment, while presence of mind opens the door to escape.

content.prompt: The power of words and wit
content.answer: Ausable defeats an armed enemy without a single weapon — only words. His stories are crafted so carefully that Max believes them and traps himself. The story teaches that language and wit are powerful tools: the person who can think and speak well can overcome brute force, and that a clever story, told with confidence, can be stronger than a gun.

content.prompt: Who was Ausable?
content.answer: Ausable was a secret agent, fat and unimpressive in appearance, living in a small room in a Paris hotel.

content.prompt: Who was Fowler and what did he expect?
content.answer: Fowler was a young writer who hoped to meet a glamorous secret agent and see real adventure, but found Ausable disappointingly ordinary.

content.prompt: How did Max enter Ausable's room?
content.answer: Max entered with a gun through the door, having come to take a report he believed was in Ausable's room.

content.prompt: What story did Ausable invent about the balcony?
content.answer: He claimed his room had a balcony running along the wall to the next room's window, which no one had dared to use because it was dangerous.

content.prompt: Why did Max climb out of the window?
content.answer: Max believed the police were knocking and, fearing arrest, tried to escape via the "balcony" — which did not exist.

content.prompt: What happened to Max?
content.answer: He stepped out of the window and fell to his death from the sixth floor, with a cry and a thud below.

content.prompt: Who was knocking at the door at the end?
content.answer: It was a waiter, who had come about Ausable's dinner — the knock that Max believed was the police.

content.prompt: What was Ausable's "secret"?
content.answer: His secret was that being too fat to act quickly, he had learned to think fast — his mind was his weapon.

content.prompt: How did Ausable outwit Max?
content.answer: Ausable outwitted Max purely with words and presence of mind. Though taken by surprise, he immediately began to talk: he pretended to be annoyed that the report had not arrived, telling Max it would be delivered shortly — a promise that kept Max calm and gave Ausable time. Then he casually mentioned the "balcony" outside his window, describing it as a dangerous route that ran to the next room, which nobody had dared to use. Max, impressed by Ausable's coolness, began to doubt himself. The masterstroke came when Ausable claimed to hear a knock and declared it must be the police coming to arrest Max. Terrified, Max bolted for the "balcony", never stopping to verify it — and fell six storeys to his death. The report, of course, never existed; the balcony never existed; and the "police" were a waiter. Ausable won by making his enemy believe his inventions, turning Max's fear against him.

content.prompt: What lesson does the story teach about appearances?
content.answer: The story teaches that appearances are deeply deceptive. Ausable looks like the last man you would call a secret agent: fat, sloppy, speaking with an accent and living in a cramped room, his mind apparently on dinner. Fowler, expecting romance and glamour, is bitterly disappointed. Yet when the crisis comes, this "ordinary" man out-thinks an armed intruder and wins with nothing but his wits. Meanwhile, the dangerous Max — all menace and gun — is revealed to be gullible and nervous, destroyed by his own fear. The lesson is that we should not judge people, or situations, by surfaces: courage, intelligence and resourcefulness are invisible qualities, and the most unremarkable-looking person may prove the most capable when it matters.

content.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about dealing with fear and crisis?
content.answer: The story teaches that fear, not the enemy, is often the greatest danger. Max was armed and in control, but his fear of the police made him abandon his advantage and leap to his death; his imagination did what Ausable's gunless hands could never have done. Ausable, in contrast, refused to panic. Faced with a gun, he did not fight or flee — he thought, spoke calmly and built a story so convincing that his enemy trapped himself. The values the story teaches are presence of mind, self-control and the courage to stay calm under pressure. In any crisis, the person who masters fear can think clearly and find a way out, while panic blinds and destroys. Ausable's quiet remark that being too fat to act quickly forced him to think fast is the moral in miniature: our weaknesses, understood and used wisely, can become our strengths.

content.prompt: Describe the character of Ausable with examples from the story.
content.answer: Ausable is a brilliant study in contrasts. Outwardly he is comical: fat, sloppy, living in a cramped sixth-floor room, speaking with an accent and preoccupied with his dinner order — Fowler even wonders how such a man became a spy. Yet this unimpressive exterior hides a mind of extraordinary quickness. When Max appears with a gun, Ausable shows no panic: he feigns annoyance, spins the tale of the missing report, and casually plants the story of the dangerous balcony. Each invention is tailored to Max's psychology — calm authority to overawe him, a mention of danger to unnerve him, and finally the "police" knock to terrify him into fleeing. His wit shines in his final confession: being too fat to act quickly, he learned to think fast. Ausable's character teaches that real strength is invisible — the quietest man, armed with presence of mind, can defeat the loudest threat.

content.prompt: Why did Fowler feel disappointed with Ausable, and how did his opinion change?
content.answer: Fowler came expecting a James Bond figure — a glamorous secret agent surrounded by mystery and adventure. Instead he found Ausable: fat, sloppy, middle-aged, living in a cramped room and concerned with ordering dinner. Fowler's disappointment is complete; he feels cheated of the romance of espionage. But the night's events transform his opinion entirely. He watches Ausable face an armed intruder with total calm, weave an elaborate fiction — the balcony, the report, the police knock — and send the enemy to his death without raising a finger. At the end, Fowler's awe is genuine: he has witnessed real heroism, which has nothing to do with appearance and everything to do with intelligence and nerve. His change of view is the reader's lesson: adventure and greatness are found not in style, but in substance.
